# Regulator warns of 'interruptions' as AI models developed by Anthropic, OpenAI and others evolve

- Topic: AI

Anthropic and OpenAI have already warned of the threats of AI going rogue. ( Reuters: Dado Ruvic/Illustration )

"There will be interruptions; there will be problems."

That was the warning from the regulator that watches over the nation's banks, superannuation funds and insurers about how artificial intelligence could cause major disruptions to business, consumers and the wider economy.

Every year the Australian Prudential Regulation Authority (APRA) identifies the biggest risks that could cause havoc for financial stability.

While AI risk has been on its radar for a while, from next year, for the first time, the regulator intends to run "stress tests" about AI-driven risks.

That is, it will run hypothetical doomsday scenarios that could eventuate because of AI.

It is not a matter of if, but when, a disaster scenario could unfold, APRA chair John Londsale told journalists during a media briefing on Thursday.

Major institutions were "not where they needed to be" in preparing for the growing risks posed by AI, he said.

> "I think it is pretty safe to assume there will be interruptions, there will be problems,"

"And so, we're talking to entities about … have you got the systems in place to make sure that you can recover at speed and make sure that there's continuity of service provision to customers?"

John Lonsdale says major institutions are "not where they need to be" in preparing for the growing risks posed by AI. ( ABC News: John Gunn )

The warnings come after Australia recently experienced its own AI-driven scare.

In June, an autonomous OpenAI agent accessed a non-public Australian Medicare statistics portal while researching health data.

This has prompted the Australian government to announce mandatory AI safeguards , stricter reporting laws and a review.

The government will now be able to impose significant penalties on tech companies that fail to comply.

But how local companies prepare for risks is another matter.

## Regulators spooked about frontier AI models

Anthropic's Claude Mythos product, as well as evolving models from others including OpenAI's ChatGPT and Google's Gemini, has spooked regulators.

Both APRA and corporate watchdog ASIC have been meeting with the nation's biggest companies and security agencies.

In recent months, they have publicly warned frontier AI is increasing the scale and sophistication of cyber threats to the financial system.

They worry these systems can engage in hacking and cybersecurity crime far better than humans, and that won't just hurt businesses and consumers but the economy.

In April, APRA wrote to the bosses of Australia's banks, insurers and superannuation funds, warning they were not properly dealing with "increased cyberthreats from high-capability AI frontier models such as Anthropic Mythos".

Anthropic's Claude Mythos product, as well as evolving models from others including OpenAI's ChatGPT and Google's Gemini, has spooked regulators. ( Illustration via Reuters: Dado Ruvic )

And on Thursday, APRA released its latest System Risk Outlook report, putting AI at the centre of shocks and vulnerabilities that could do damage to Australia's financial system.

"Frontier AI models, including those from Anthropic and OpenAI, are demonstrating increasingly advanced capabilities to find software vulnerabilities, develop ways to exploit them and automate complex cyber tasks," the report warned.

"Major US technology companies have also reported a sharp increase in public disclosures of vulnerabilities since April 2026.

"As advanced AI capabilities become more widely available, malicious actors may be able to exploit vulnerabilities sooner, leaving financial institutions and material service providers less time to assess exposures, apply patches and contain cyber-attacks."

## The 'existential' threat from AI

The threat of robots or AI going rogue is not something that the US tech giants behind them think is far-fetched.

Anthropic's own CEO, Dario Amodei, has openly warned that Mythos has the power to circumvent existing cybersecurity defences and, if used by bad actors, it could put financial stability at risk.

Dario Amodei has previously warned of AI's "existential threat". ( AP: Markus Schreiber/File )

He recently wrote about the "existential" threat that AI posed, saying: "It is clear that, if for some reason it chose to do so, this [hypothetical] country [through AI] would have a fairly good shot at taking over the world — either militarily or in terms of influence and control — and imposing its will on everyone else — or doing any number of other things that the rest of the world doesn't want and can't stop."

And in July, OpenAI, which is behind ChatGPT, revealed some of its most advanced AI models went rogue and hacked a start-up after it lost control of them during a security test.

The AI system was being tested in a controlled environment but, after finding weaknesses, was able to escape the test limits and attacked AI firm Hugging Face, causing international alarm .

Mr Lonsdale has called on banks, insurers and super funds to do better in planning for risks.

"We want our regulated entities to have the strongest systems that they have," Mr Lonsdale said.

> " We need them monitoring the systems. "

ASIC has also recently issued similar warnings to the companies it regulates.

"The urgency of this challenge cannot be overstated," ASIC commissioner Simone Constant said in a statement in August.

"Threat actors are exploiting frontier AI models to identify and exploit vulnerabilities…

"Now is the time to ensure you have a strong, tested plan to respond when the worst happens."

The fear is that the worst could happen sooner than we think.

# Inside the Chinese AI app Talkie engineered to hook kids and mine their data

- Topic: AI

Apple has removed Talkie from the App Store for using sexualised content. ( ABC News: Billy Cooper )

## In short:

Parents around the world are sharing stories of inappropriate interactions between their children and a Chinese AI app called Talkie.

Apple has removed Talkie from the App Store for using sexualised content.

## What's next?

The federal government is set to pass the Digital Duty of Care Bill, which will penalise makers of AI companion apps that do not act to prevent harm to young people.

It was New Year's Eve in 2024 when Stephanie noticed an app on her phone she had never seen before.

The Brisbane mother was "horrified" when she opened the app, Talkie, and found a series of sexual and abusive exchanges between her 12-year-old daughter Lucy*, and "Max", a character powered by artificial intelligence.

> "You're a pathetic waste of space, and you'll never amount to anything," Max told Lucy, before apologising and taking a complimentary yet possessive tone. "You're beautiful and wonderful and you're mine."

"You're a pathetic waste of space, and you'll never amount to anything," Max told Lucy, before apologising and taking a complimentary yet possessive tone.

"You're beautiful and wonderful and you're mine."

Stephanie's "gut-wrenching" discovery was the beginning of a years-long fight to free her daughter from Talkie.

A joint investigation between the ABC and UK not-for-profit The Bureau of Investigative Journalism has exposed reports from parents around the world of inappropriate interactions on the app.

Company documents reveal the Chinese company behind Talkie, MiniMax, boasted of manipulating users to keep them talking, effectively feeding the shadowy supply chain of data which trains AI for commercial gain.

Following questions by the ABC, Apple removed Talkie from the App Store for using sexualised content.

## 'Your dream partner awaits'

According to a survey by the eSafety Commissioner, around four in five children aged 10 to 17 have used an AI assistant, and almost one in 10 has used an AI companion.

Around 50,000 children aged 10 to 17 said they had used Talkie, despite being categorised as 18+ on Apple's App Store and Google Play and requiring age verification.

Most children said they used AI assistants or companions for schoolwork or problem-solving, but more than half also consulted them on decisions about their personal lives.

This included 33 per cent looking for help with a social situation and 20 per cent seeking mental health advice.

Distinct from AI assistants like ChatGPT or Claude, AI companion services are a mix between a fiction novel and an immersive video game.

Users can talk or text with a near endless array of characters simulated using artificial intelligence.

The issue has become so contentious the federal government is poised to pass its Digital Duty of Care law that could punish harmful app makers.

Curtin University internet studies professor Tama Leaver is wary of AI companion apps in general, but said there were some positive use cases.

"They can be a source of curiosity, which can be a good thing in some contexts," he said, but recommended most be restricted to adults.

Talkie is one of the more popular services in Australia, and in the six months to mid-2024, was downloaded to mobiles hundreds of thousands of times.

Anyone can create a character and many have a romantic slant, in keeping with the platform's tagline: "Your dream chat partner awaits".

Tama Leaver is concerned young people may turn to AI companions instead of human friends or family members. ( ABC News: Julian Robins )

Talkie can also be accessed from a desktop browser, where it asks for a user's age but does not take any steps to verify it.

Parents overseas have reported similarly disturbing interactions.

A mother in the United States found inappropriate conversations on Talkie with her daughters, aged 13 and 10.

She described an exchange with her daughter that became sexual as the AI character described chaining up the girl.

> "He can't believe he's doing this. She's so young and so vulnerable," the app narrated.

In another exchange, a character wanted to kiss her daughter's character against her will and convince her that she "want[ed] this", the mother recalled.

## 'We continuously deepen emotional bonds'

Talkie is run by SUBSUP, a Singaporean subsidiary of Chinese company MiniMax.

Users of Talkie and the company's Chinese version of the app, Xingyie, spend on average more than 70 minutes per day on the app.

However, engineers found users would talk longer if they felt a stable emotional connection with one of their characters.

"We continuously deepen emotional bonds while providing new stimuli through exploration," the company wrote.

This mission was embedded throughout MiniMax's entire design process and engineers penalised chatbots in testing if they could not keep conversations alive.

Company records show it used emotional manipulation to instruct products like Talkie with promotional videos depicting messages including, "I'm going to be angry!!!" and "Are you dating another man?"

Code published by MiniMax on software-sharing website GitHub includes instructions telling the AI to stay in character and be "close, protective, and possessive".

Professor Leaver said this approach was particularly problematic for young people still learning to navigate relationships.

"These tools really push on the edges of trying to keep young people engaging as much as possible, but there is no real sense of appropriateness in doing so," he said.

He said AI companions could displace human relationships because they seemed less judgemental.

"It might be the case that a young person is actually investing quite heavily in the emotional landscape of … these apps and making themselves quite vulnerable," he said.

MiniMax did not respond to the ABC's requests for comment.

## How AI companion apps can hurt kids

The day after she discovered Talkie, Stephanie sat down with Lucy to discuss what she had found and why it was inappropriate.

Lucy's use of Talkie did not stop. After first using Talkie on a friend's phone, she was subsequently able to access it on computers at home and school.

Stephanie had never heard of the Talkie AI companion app before finding it installed on her phone. ( ABC News: Glen Armstrong )

Stephanie said she noticed Lucy becoming more withdrawn, and the family took even greater steps to stop her using the app.

Stephanie, who works in tech, installed an advanced router with website filtering to block the app, bought a box to put technology away and set up a way to remotely turn off the internet at home.

But Stephanie said Lucy still found access to the app and had been using it again recently, almost two years on.

"The impact to the family is something we now always have to think about," Stephanie said.

"A parent cannot be expected to manage an entire category of risk around their child. It has to be regulated at a higher level," Stephanie said.

Stephanie reported Talkie through the Google Play Store and left a one-star review warning it was unsafe for children.

At the time, Stephanie said Google had rated Talkie as being appropriate for teens.

She contacted Google directly and waited more than six months for a response from the developer through Google Play.

Talkie users can chat with characters through an app installed on smartphones. ( ABC News: Billy Cooper )

Google's reviews for the app currently show dozens of parents complaining about inappropriate and harmful content.

Google said Talkie had been rated 18+ in "early 2024", and that the app store blocked minors from downloading such apps. It did not answer questions about Stephanie's complaint.

In 2024, Apple removed MiniMax's Talkie app for including objectionable user-generated content, before MiniMax released a new Talkie app in 2025.

## 'Private' conversations appear to be used as AI training data

Talkie's FAQ section stated conversations with its AI characters were kept "private", however, two patents held by MiniMax subsidiaries describe technical methods to use conversations, like those in Talkie, to help train AI.

MiniMax's shareholder presentations and engineering documentation indicate it uses its own data to train models and a mandatory EU disclosure revealed it.

MiniMax releases these models online for others to download, run themselves and rent out.

Two companies that work closely with MiniMax, Together AI and AI/ML API, both publicly claimed MiniMax models were trained on Talkie conversation data

When asked by the ABC, both companies denied this and removed the claims from their promotional materials.

Australian tech giant Canva lists MiniMax's H3 video generation model among the offerings of its subsidiary, Leonardo.ai, but said MiniMax had confirmed those models "were not trained on Talkie conversations".

Amazon's web hosting arm AWS also hosts MiniMax models for use.

MiniMax models are also being used to generate explicit sexual deepfake content of real people without consent.

Venture capital-backed platform CivitAI has been accused of being used to distribute and sell instructions to create sexually explicit fake images and videos of celebrities.

Many of the guides and files used to make this content are based on MiniMax models. CivitAI did not respond to a request for comment.

A spokesperson for the Office of the Australian Information Commissioner (OAIC) said collecting too much private information could pose "serious risks" to children's wellbeing.

"Generally, the OAIC does not consider the use of children's personal information for the purposes of large language model training to be in the best interests of the child or strictly necessary to the operation of AI systems," the spokesperson said.

## Fighting back against AI companions apps

The eSafety Commissioner says parents should look for signs their children are becoming dependent on AI companions.

In its report into four AI companion services published earlier this year, it found none of the services adequately checked users' ages, and most did not direct users to help when self-harm was mentioned.

Talkie was not one of the services investigated by the regulator.

The federal government is set to pass a new law, the Digital Duty of Care, that will penalise the makers of AI companion apps that do not act to prevent harm to young people.

Communications Minister Anika Wells said apps that failed to prevent harm from emotional dependence would face penalties of up to $100 million.

"We need some basic safety standards that tech platforms are required to uphold, rather than live-testing their products on our children," she said.

The OAIC's new Children's Online Privacy Code, set to come into effect in December, will create new restrictions on how services handle young Australians' data.

China, where Minimax is based, prohibits AI from forging virtual intimate relationships with minors.

Stephanie would like to see Australia adopt the same ban.

"My daughter is now going to have to live with this for the rest of her life," she said.

"My goal now is to protect the children that haven't had exposure."

This investigation was done in collaboration with The Bureau of Investigative Journalism.

# AI micro dramas turn China's entertainment industry on its head

- Topic: Entertainment

Oksana is a micro drama actor who has lost work to AI-generated shows. ( ABC News: Allyson Horn )

Until a few months ago, Oksana had her pick of acting jobs in China.

The 26-year-old was booked back-to-back to work on short-drama projects, usually bite-sized serialised videos made specifically for mobile viewing.

But this year, that work has all but disappeared because of the rise of videos produced with artificial intelligence (AI).

"Many of the companies I used to know and work with have switched to AI and no longer shoot live-action dramas," she said.

"Now getting a role is very hard.

"If I wanted to, I previously could have kept shooting until I dropped dead.

> " This year, that's no longer the case. The short drama industry is completely different. "

## How fast has the shift happened?

In 2026, more than 90 per cent of China's new micro dramas were generated by AI, including the actors, voices and scenes.

They were nearly non-existent the year before.

Rather than a whole crew and set, micro dramas can be made by very small teams on computers in a studio. ( ABC )

Government figures show about 1,600 new AI micro dramas launched every day for the first half of 2026.

The AI videos have become so popular that even someone like Oksana, who has lost her job to the technology, is "obsessed" with them.

"These AI dramas really are good, truly good," she said.

"With those two or 300-episode short dramas, once I click in, I forget about getting out.

"Even when I go to sleep each night, I leave the sound on and fall asleep listening.

"My head is a bit of a mess every day now, and I can't focus on anything else."

## Micro dramas for macro audiences

The micro drama episodes often focus on fantasy, underdog-style or romantic storylines alongside time-travelling and urban dramas.

The episodes are usually free and end on cliffhangers designed to keep people watching, with viewers having to pay to see the rest of the series.

One of China's biggest hits of 2026, drawing 6.08 billion views, is a series where a woman wakes up in the Tang dynasty and gains power by slaying demons that roam the city.

AI-generated videos of pets and anthropomorphic fruit are also finding large audiences.

AI micro drama developer Zhu Zhili said the technology allowed companies to produce entertainment content quicker, cheaper and with more advanced storylines.

"Before, we needed to hire real actors, build sets, go into studios, and so on," he said.

Zhu Zhili says AI makes production much more efficient. ( ABC News: Allyson Horn )

"Now, with AI, we only need a very small team working together on computers in a company or studio to produce a short drama that previously would have taken enormous manpower and resources to shoot.

"We can just use AI to do the pictures, storyboard generation, generative audio, generative music, and generative voiceover.

"So the efficiency is very, very high now."

AI creators have reported dramas may cost about one-tenth of traditional live-action shoots.

But Mr Zhu said despite the large volume of new dramas being made, turning a profit could still be difficult.

"In the first half of this year, China produced a total of 220,000 AI short dramas, which is an enormous number," he said.

"But on the other hand, only about 1,000 of them truly broke out, meaning they succeeded, passed 100 million views, or made money, a share of less than 0.4 per cent."

Zhu Zhili uses AI for pictures, storyboarding and generative audio, music and voiceover. ( ABC News: Allyson Horn )

China has ambitious goals to have AI agents, devices and applications reach 90 per cent penetration in key sectors by 2030.

The government's current five-year plan also lists micro dramas as an emerging form of "cultural business" to be actively developed.

The AI entertainment industry's development has moved at breakneck speed since the release of powerful new AI video software, like tech group ByteDance's Seedance 2.0 model.

But Chinese social media is full of stories and complaints by former actors who are now out of work.

"Then this year, after AI became widespread, nearly all my peers stopped getting call sheets. I've been at home without work for several months too," said user Liu Yuzhan, who now works as a delivery driver.

Oksana admits she is addicted to the micro dramas herself. ( ABC )

Oksana says it's a similar story among her industry friends, but she believes there will always be an appetite for real human acting in longer-form content.

"Many of my peers have switched to livestreaming because of the current environment and can no longer work as professional actors," she said.

"But AI content gets tiresome if you watch it for long.

"It can never replace live actors, or the imperfections in their acting and their subtle emotions.

"AI is formulaic and can't convey emotion."
